When the world, the state, and the family are brought back to oneself, it is said: “That by which these are put into practice is one.” These words, spoken by the Master to Duke Ai of Lu, served to expand upon the government of Kings Wen and Wu, but in truth established a standard for the Way of the ruler for ten thousand generations.

Now, the ruler is but a single person, while the world, the state, and the family are vast, and their people exceedingly numerous. The worthy, his kin, the great ministers, the assembled officials, the common people, the various artisans, people from afar, and the feudal lords—the things they depend upon him to supply are bewilderingly diverse. For a single person to wield such immense power, govern so many people, and seek to bring unity to their exceedingly diverse dispositions—how could clever techniques, laws, and ordinances accomplish this? Surely it is simply a matter of following the principles inherent in them and having the means oneself to respond to them; of following the due portion with which each is endowed and having the means oneself to provide for them. Only when I have the means to respond to them and provide for them can this be achieved. Thus, if one seeks it in the world, the state, and the family instead of seeking it in oneself…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
也祇見其日騖于叢瑣而不可爲也已誠知夫
天下國家之人即一人也一人之身即天下國
家之身也如是而視吾身如是而視天下國家
使我與天下國家共爲一體元氣充滿流行而
四肢百骸莫不相貫視聽持行罔不相用無有
壅塞凌悖間隔而不通之處是爲大公而無我
大公而無我故能順應而不窮斯吾身與天下
國家並理之至術也噫身爲本一爲要焉所謂
一者豈出于夫子所言哉夫子前此曰脩身以
===
道脩道以仁仁者人也後此則曰誠身誠者天
之道也自天而言謂之誠自人而言謂之仁誠
非仁之肫肫乎仁非誠之生生乎天道誠也而
其一元之氣運行不息其始萬物者元也其品
物流形爲亨元之流形也其變化既成萬物爲
利貞即元之變化也曰復其見天地之心曰天
地之大德曰生天地之心何嘗一日而不生物
哉天命流行物與無妄吾身之所自來也屬之
于心則曰人得天地生物之心以爲心然則夫
punctuated: 也，祇見其日騖于叢瑣而不可爲也已。誠知夫天下國家之人即一人也，一人之身即天下國家之身也，如是而視吾身，如是而視天下國家，使我與天下國家共爲一體，元氣充滿流行，而四肢百骸莫不相貫，視聽持行罔不相用，無有壅塞凌悖、間隔而不通之處，是爲大公而無我。大公而無我，故能順應而不窮，斯吾身與天下國家並理之至術也。噫！身爲本，一爲要焉。所謂一者，豈出于夫子所言哉？夫子前此曰：「脩身以道，脩道以仁。仁者，人也。」後此則曰：「誠身。」「誠者，天之道也。」自天而言謂之誠，自人而言謂之仁。誠非仁之肫肫乎？仁非誠之生生乎？天道誠也，而其一元之氣運行不息。其始萬物者，元也；其品物流形爲亨，元之流形也；其變化既成萬物爲利貞，即元之變化也。曰：「復，其見天地之心。」曰：「天地之大德曰生。」天地之心何嘗一日而不生物哉？天命流行，物與無妄，吾身之所自來也。屬之于心，則曰：「人得天地生物之心以爲心。」然則夫
translation_en:
…one will only find oneself daily chasing a mass of petty details, unable to accomplish anything. Truly understand that the people of the world, the state, and the family are one person, and that the body of one person is the body of the world, the state, and the family. Regard oneself in this way, and regard the world, the state, and the family in this way, so that oneself and all of them together form a single body. Its primal vital force fills it and circulates throughout; its four limbs and hundred bones are all interconnected, and seeing, hearing, grasping, and walking all serve one another. Nowhere is there obstruction, disorder, separation, or failure of communication. This is supreme impartiality and freedom from self. Because one is supremely impartial and free from self, one can respond fittingly without exhaustion. This is the ultimate method for bringing order both to oneself and to the world, the state, and the family.

Ah! The self is the foundation, and unity is the essential point. Could what is meant by unity lie outside what the Master said? Earlier, the Master says: “Cultivate the self through the Way, and cultivate the Way through benevolence. Benevolence is being human.” Later, he says: “Make oneself sincere,” and “Sincerity is the Way of Heaven.” Spoken of in terms of Heaven, it is called sincerity; spoken of in terms of humanity, it is called benevolence. Is sincerity not the profound earnestness of benevolence? Is benevolence not the ceaseless generative activity of sincerity? Heaven’s Way is sincerity, and its unitary primal vital force circulates without rest. That which initiates the myriad things is origination. The various kinds of things flowing into form constitute flourishing: this is origination flowing into form. Their transformations, once they have brought the myriad things to completion, constitute benefit and constancy: these are the transformations of origination.

It is said: “In Return, one sees the heart of Heaven and Earth.” It is also said: “The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called generation.” Has the heart of Heaven and Earth ever gone a single day without generating things? Heaven’s mandate flows onward, and things partake of freedom from falsity; this is the source from which my own being comes. In relation to the heart, it is said: “Human beings receive the life-generating heart of Heaven and Earth as their own heart.” Thus, then, the Master…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
子所謂誠與仁者非二也卽所謂一也此理在
人渾然無欲粹然不雜謂之至善能明善則能
誠身誠身卽仁其身也能仁其身則吾身爲德
之聚而達德非三也爲道之管而達道非五也
爲人之存而文武非爲先也故能視天下國家
之人惟我而視我惟人凡人之有所取足于我
者我皆有以順其性平其情不違其所願而與
之各得其所賢者吾有以尊之義之所以盡也
親者吾有以親之仁之所以至也于大臣敬之
===
于羣臣體之庶民子之百工來之遠人諸侯則
柔之懷之何莫而非親親之殺尊賢之等也禮
之所以達也故曰所以行之者一也是爲天下
國家之常經而二帝三王之所不能易者也稽
諸陶唐氏睦族和邦授時釐工莫非經也而實
堯之明德能仁其身爲之稽諸有虞氏齊政輯
瑞詢岳命官莫非經也而實舜之精一能仁其
身爲之夏商以來六事之治五服之制人紀之
脩官刑之儆莫非經也而實禹湯之好善執中
punctuated:
子所謂誠與仁者，非二也，卽所謂一也。此理在人，渾然無欲，粹然不雜，謂之至善。能明善，則能誠身；誠身，卽仁其身也。能仁其身，則吾身爲德之聚，而達德非三也；爲道之管，而達道非五也；爲人之存，而文武非爲先也。故能視天下國家之人惟我，而視我惟人。凡人之有所取足于我者，我皆有以順其性，平其情，不違其所願，而與之各得其所。賢者，吾有以尊之，義之所以盡也；親者，吾有以親之，仁之所以至也。于大臣敬之，于羣臣體之，庶民子之，百工來之，遠人諸侯則柔之懷之，何莫而非親親之殺、尊賢之等也？禮之所以達也。故曰：「所以行之者一也。」是爲天下國家之常經，而二帝三王之所不能易者也。
稽諸陶唐氏，睦族和邦，授時釐工，莫非經也，而實堯之明德能仁其身爲之。稽諸有虞氏，齊政輯瑞，詢岳命官，莫非經也，而實舜之精一能仁其身爲之。夏商以來，六事之治，五服之制，人紀之脩，官刑之儆，莫非經也，而實禹湯之好善執中
translation_en:
…What the Master calls sincerity and benevolence are not two things: they are precisely what he calls the one. In human beings, this principle is whole and free of desire, pure and unmixed; this is called the highest good. If one can understand goodness, one can make oneself sincere; making oneself sincere is precisely making oneself benevolent. If I can make myself benevolent, my person becomes the gathering place of virtue, and the universally applicable virtues are no longer three separate things; it becomes the governing center of the Way, and the universally applicable relationships are no longer five separate things; it embodies the presence of the requisite person, and Kings Wen and Wu have no precedence over me. Thus I can regard the people of the world, the state, and the family as myself, and myself as others. Whatever others look to me to supply, I have the means to accord with their natures, bring harmony to their feelings, and, without frustrating their wishes, enable each to find their proper place. I have the means to honor the worthy: through this, righteousness is fully realized. I have the means to cherish my kin: through this, benevolence reaches its utmost. I respect the great ministers and put myself in the position of the assembled officials; I treat the common people as my children and attract the various artisans; I extend kindness to people from afar and cherish the feudal lords. Which of these does not express the diminishing degrees of affection for kin and the graduated honors accorded to the worthy? Through these, ritual propriety finds full expression. Thus it is said: “That by which they are put into practice is one.” These are the constant norms for the world, the state, and the family, which even the Two Emperors and Three Kings could not alter.
Consider the ruler of Taotang: bringing concord to his clan and harmony to the states, promulgating the seasons, and regulating the various tasks—all were applications of these norms. Yet it was truly Yao’s luminous virtue, by which he made himself benevolent, that accomplished them. Consider the ruler of Youyu: ordering celestial affairs, collecting the jade credentials, consulting the Four Peaks, and appointing officials—all were applications of these norms. Yet it was truly Shun’s refinement and single-mindedness, by which he made himself benevolent, that accomplished them. From the Xia and Shang onward, government through the six affairs, the system of five territorial zones, the cultivation of human relationships, and the warnings embodied in punishments for officials—all were applications of these norms. Yet it was truly Yu’s and Tang’s love of goodness and adherence to the mean…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
耶與人一己百人十己千之說皆爲哀公設也
而夫子之情亦激矣不然九經之章吾道一以
貫之一言而足何樂乎其詞之費也夫不灼其
形眛者弗覩不烈其聲灇者弗聞灼其形烈其
聲而猶弗覩弗聞如哀公夫子且奈之何噫九
經之義昭然漢以霸蝕唐以夷棄宋未盡行明
而行之不能無待于知人知天者
表
擬宋宣撫使狄青平廣南羣臣賀表〔皇祐〕
===
〔五年〕
洪敷誥
同考試官教諭梁 批狄青崑崙之捷場中能悉
其故實者絶少獨此作敘事詳明摛詞典雅且忠
愛之誠盎然可掬非特四六之工已也
考試官教諭陳 批體裁莊整詞藻煥發
考試官教授王 批駢麗可則
皇祐五年宣撫使狄青大破蠻賊儂智高
于邕州廣南悉平臣某等謹奉
punctuated:
耶？與「人一己百，人十己千」之說，皆爲哀公設也，而夫子之情亦激矣。不然，九經之章，「吾道一以貫之」一言而足，何樂乎其詞之費也？夫不灼其形，眛者弗覩；不烈其聲，灇者弗聞。灼其形，烈其聲，而猶弗覩弗聞，如哀公，夫子且奈之何？噫！九經之義昭然，漢以霸蝕，唐以夷棄，宋未盡行。明而行之，不能無待于知人知天者。
表
擬宋宣撫使狄青平廣南羣臣賀表〔皇祐〕〔五年〕
洪敷誥
同考試官教諭梁批：狄青崑崙之捷，場中能悉其故實者絶少。獨此作敘事詳明，摛詞典雅，且忠愛之誠盎然可掬，非特四六之工已也。
考試官教諭陳批：體裁莊整，詞藻煥發。
考試官教授王批：駢麗可則。
皇祐五年，宣撫使狄青大破蠻賊儂智高于邕州，廣南悉平。臣某等謹奉
translation_en:
…? Together with the saying, “What others accomplish with one effort, I will accomplish with a hundred; what others accomplish with ten, I will accomplish with a thousand,” these words were all addressed specifically to Duke Ai, and the Master's feelings, too, were deeply stirred. Otherwise, for the chapter on the nine guiding principles, the single statement “My Way is threaded through by one principle” would have sufficed. Why would he have delighted in such expenditure of words? Unless a form is made brilliant, those with dim sight cannot see it; unless a sound is made forceful, those hard of hearing [?] cannot hear it. If, even when the form is brilliant and the sound forceful, someone still neither sees nor hears—as with Duke Ai—what could the Master do with him? Alas! The meaning of the nine guiding principles is manifest. The Han eroded it through hegemonic rule; the Tang abandoned it through barbarian ways; the Song did not fully put it into practice. Understanding and implementing it must still depend upon those who understand human beings and Heaven.
Memorial
A simulated congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials on the Song Pacification Commissioner Di Qing's pacification of Guangnan 〔Huangyou〕〔fifth year〕
Hong Fugao
Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Instructor: Very few candidates in the examination hall knew all the historical particulars of Di Qing's victory at Kunlun. This composition alone narrates the events fully and clearly, and its diction is classically elegant. Moreover, its sincere loyalty and devotion overflow so abundantly that one could almost gather them in one's hands. Its accomplishment is by no means confined to skill in four-and-six parallel prose.
Comment by Examiner Chen, Instructor: The form is dignified and orderly; the diction is brilliant.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Professor: Its elegant parallel prose may serve as a model.
In the fifth year of Huangyou, Pacification Commissioner Di Qing decisively defeated the barbarian rebel Nong Zhigao at Yongzhou, and all of Guangnan was pacified. We, your servants So-and-so and the others, respectfully present …

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
表稱
賀者伏以
六師雷動隼旟指翼軫以南征五嶺風清
鰲極控湖湘而北奠運
謨猷于帷幄銷氛祲於潢池捷
獻崑崙歡騰河洛臣某等誠懽誠忭稽首頓
首竊惟虞帝嚴猾夏之防士師敕法周官
重攘夷之略司馬專征舞干羽于七旬有
苗來格勤師徒於六月獫狁于襄蓋人主
===
守在四夷用昭文德以威不軌而天王治
大一統當除戎器以戒不虞粤若嶺南寔
稱邊徼在虞周尚違聲教至秦漢始入職
方馬援收徵側之勛百蠻褫魄任囂諭蒼
梧之詔列郡歸心迨有唐既疲河北之師
致中葉遂墮日南之績夷酋跋扈勢有類
乎鴟張險阻憑陵衆實同于蟻聚自昔乍
臣而乍叛伊誰七縱而七擒顧
今海內為家豈容榻邊思鼾
punctuated:
表稱賀者，伏以六師雷動，隼旟指翼軫以南征；五嶺風清，鰲極控湖湘而北奠。運謨猷于帷幄，銷氛祲於潢池；捷獻崑崙，歡騰河洛。臣某等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首。
竊惟虞帝嚴猾夏之防，士師敕法；周官重攘夷之略，司馬專征。舞干羽于七旬，有苗來格；勤師徒於六月，獫狁于襄。蓋人主守在四夷，用昭文德以威不軌；而天王治大一統，當除戎器以戒不虞。粤若嶺南，寔稱邊徼。在虞周尚違聲教，至秦漢始入職方。馬援收徵側之勛，百蠻褫魄；任囂諭蒼梧之詔，列郡歸心。迨有唐既疲河北之師，致中葉遂墮日南之績。夷酋跋扈，勢有類乎鴟張；險阻憑陵，衆實同于蟻聚。自昔乍臣而乍叛，伊誰七縱而七擒？顧今海內為家，豈容榻邊思鼾？
translation_en:
…a memorial offering congratulations, humbly declaring: The Six Armies move like thunder; their falcon banners point toward the constellations Yi and Zhen as they campaign southward. The winds are clear over the Five Ranges; the imperial pole, supported by the great turtle, commands Hu and Xiang and stands securely to the north. Strategies are devised within the command tent, and the baleful vapors of rebellion are dispersed from the shallow pools. News of victory at Kunlun is presented, and rejoicing rises throughout the He and Luo regions. Your servants, so-and-so and the others, truly joyful and truly delighted, bow low and knock their heads upon the ground.
We humbly reflect that the emperor of Yu strictly guarded against disturbances to the Xia realm, and his Judge enforced the laws; the offices of Zhou gave weight to strategies for repelling the non-Chinese peoples, and the Minister of War exercised authority over punitive campaigns. After dances with shields and pheasant plumes for seventy days, the Youmiao came to submit; when the troops labored in the sixth month, the Xianyun were driven away. For a ruler’s defenses lie among the peoples of the four quarters: he displays civil virtue to overawe those who defy order. The Son of Heaven governs a unified realm: he must keep weapons ready against unforeseen dangers.
As for Lingnan, it is indeed a borderland. In the days of Yu and Zhou it still lay beyond the reach of imperial instruction; only under Qin and Han did it enter the administrative domain. Ma Yuan won distinction by subduing Zheng Ce, striking terror into the many southern peoples; Ren Xiao proclaimed an edict to Cangwu [?], and the commanderies gave their allegiance. By the Tang dynasty, however, the armies had already been exhausted in Hebei, so that by the middle of the dynasty the achievements in Rinan had fallen away. The non-Chinese chieftains grew overbearing, their power like that of an owl spreading its wings; relying on difficult terrain, they encroached, their multitudes gathering like ants. Since ancient times they have alternated between submission and rebellion: who could release them seven times and capture them seven times? Yet now that all within the seas forms one household, how could anyone be allowed to contemplate snoring beside the imperial couch? …

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
共難釋周文之赫怒上廑
宵旰博訪安攘紓籌策於
九重兼聽輿人之誦聞鼓鼙于四境爰思將帥
之遺迺
命樞貳之重臣俾膺經略之大任
綸紼自天而下
制重登壇牙旗向日而開
命隆專閫鷹鸇奮擊乘雲氣而度斗南貔虎成
羣挾風聲而踰嶺表晡傳蓐食宵下險關
===
嚴陳曙失律之誅三軍股栗鼓賈逵先登
之勇羣醜魂搖驅精銳以摧其前席卷建
瓴之勢麾蕃落直擣於後刃迎破竹之鋒
彼黨方豕突而狼奔我師咸投石而超距
追亡百里山川震逐北之威俘馘萬人草
木動征西之氣殲厥醜類固我封疆救民
水火之中室家胥慶旋師枕席之上簞食
來迎士已樂乎投戈野咸安於負耒追蹤
銅柱紀不世奇勳奏績
punctuated: 共難釋周文之赫怒，上廑宵旰，博訪安攘，紓籌策於九重，兼聽輿人之誦，聞鼓鼙于四境，爰思將帥之遺，迺命樞貳之重臣，俾膺經略之大任。綸紼自天而下，制重登壇；牙旗向日而開，命隆專閫。鷹鸇奮擊，乘雲氣而度斗南；貔虎成羣，挾風聲而踰嶺表。晡傳蓐食，宵下險關。嚴陳曙失律之誅，三軍股栗；鼓賈逵先登之勇，羣醜魂搖。驅精銳以摧其前，席卷建瓴之勢；麾蕃落直擣於後，刃迎破竹之鋒。彼黨方豕突而狼奔，我師咸投石而超距。追亡百里，山川震逐北之威；俘馘萬人，草木動征西之氣。殲厥醜類，固我封疆，救民水火之中，室家胥慶；旋師枕席之上，簞食來迎。士已樂乎投戈，野咸安於負耒。追蹤銅柱，紀不世奇勳；奏績
translation_en:
…[The opening phrase 共難釋 is unclear.] The blazing wrath of King Wen of Zhou stirred imperial concern, keeping Your Majesty at work before dawn and late into the night. You sought counsel widely on securing peace within and repelling threats without, deliberating upon strategies in the innermost palace and also hearing the common people's songs. Hearing the war drums on all four frontiers, you recalled the legacy of commanders of old. You therefore appointed a high minister serving as Vice Minister of War to shoulder the great responsibility of directing the campaign. The imperial command descended from Heaven, lending solemn authority to his ascent of the commander's platform; the ivory-adorned banner unfurled toward the sun, and his commission conferred the dignity of independent military command.

Hawks and falcons struck fiercely, riding the clouds across the lands south of the Dipper; troops like leopards and tigers gathered in hosts, sweeping with the wind beyond the mountain ranges. Orders were relayed at dusk, and the troops ate before rising from their bedding; by night they captured formidable passes. The stern punishment of Chen Shu for breaches of military discipline made the whole army tremble; the encouragement of courage like Jia Kui's in being first to scale the walls shook the souls of the villainous hordes. Elite troops were driven forward to crush their front, with the irresistible force of a sweeping mat or water poured from a rooftop; tribal contingents were directed straight into their rear, their blades advancing as easily as splitting bamboo. While the enemy bands charged like boars and fled like wolves, our troops all displayed their strength in stone-throwing and leaping.

They pursued the fugitives for a hundred li, and mountains and rivers shook at the might of the pursuit; ten thousand were captured or slain, and even the grasses and trees stirred at the martial spirit of the western campaign. Their vile bands were annihilated and our frontiers secured. The people were rescued from fire and water, and every household rejoiced. The army returned as easily as resting upon a pillow and mat, and people came to welcome it with baskets of food. The soldiers now rejoiced in laying down their weapons, while throughout the countryside people peacefully shouldered their ploughs. Following the precedent of the bronze pillars, extraordinary achievements unparalleled in an age were commemorated; military successes were reported…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
玉階彰曠時之偉略是皆
宸衷獨斷明威電照于域中遂令將校同心號
令風行乎閫外固將除兇而翦逆誠非黷
武以窮兵築京觀於邕南翼翼奠華夷之
界限息狼烟于甌駱明明壯百二之山河
臣等敵愾有懷憂時共念勞未伸於汗馬
柎已知慙心甞切于據鞍聞風思奮仰窺
勝筭嘆識
帝王之有真幸際凱旋知
===
仁者之無敵車騎懽呼於重譯衣冠蹈舞于
千斑伏願
駿烈覃敷
鴻恩遐曁
乃文乃武用對
帝臣之心
作福作威式敷
皇極之訓右騶虞貍首
瑶圖鞏周道於繇延朝荆楚享氐羌
punctuated:
玉階，彰曠時之偉略。是皆宸衷獨斷，明威電照于域中，遂令將校同心，號令風行乎閫外。固將除兇而翦逆，誠非黷武以窮兵。築京觀於邕南，翼翼奠華夷之界限；息狼烟于甌駱，明明壯百二之山河。
臣等敵愾有懷，憂時共念。勞未伸於汗馬，柎已知慙；心甞切于據鞍，聞風思奮。仰窺勝筭，嘆識帝王之有真；幸際凱旋，知仁者之無敵。車騎懽呼於重譯，衣冠蹈舞于千斑。伏願駿烈覃敷，鴻恩遐曁。乃文乃武，用對帝臣之心；作福作威，式敷皇極之訓。右騶虞貍首，瑶圖鞏周道於繇延，朝荆楚，享氐羌。
translation_en:
…at the jade steps of the throne, displaying magnificent strategy unequaled for generations. All this arose from Your Majesty’s independent resolve: your radiant might flashed like lightning throughout the realm, bringing commanders and officers into accord and sending orders abroad as swiftly as the wind beyond the military headquarters. The purpose was assuredly to eliminate the wicked and cut down rebels, certainly not to indulge in warfare or exhaust the troops. Mounds of enemy corpses were raised south of Yong, firmly establishing the boundary between the Chinese and the non-Chinese peoples; the beacons of war were extinguished in Ouluo, gloriously strengthening mountains and rivers whose strategic advantages enable two to withstand a hundred.
We, your servants, cherish a determination to resist the enemy and share concern for the times. We have yet to render service upon sweating warhorses, and already feel shame [the preceding 柎 is unclear]; our hearts have long yearned to mount the saddle, and news of these deeds stirs us to action. Looking reverently upon your victorious calculations, we recognize with wonder a true emperor; fortunate to witness the triumphant return, we know that the benevolent have no enemies. Charioteers and cavalrymen cheer amid peoples whose speech requires successive interpreters; officials in their caps and robes dance for joy in a thousand ranks [?]. Humbly we wish that your splendid achievements may spread everywhere and your abundant grace reach afar. Through both civil and military governance, respond to the hearts of your imperial servants; by bestowing blessings and wielding authority, disseminate the teaching of the August Ultimate. Honor [?] the songs “The Zouyu Beast” and “The Wildcat’s Head”; may your precious imperial dominion secure the way of Zhou in enduring continuity [?], bring Jing and Chu to court, and receive tribute from the Di and Qiang…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
國家文武一道威德兼隆信足以軼唐虞而媲成周者子能鋪
張惕厲以鳴其盛而純一不息之論更覘臣子忠
愛無已之情宜錄以式
考試官教授王批我
皇上嗣統覲揚光烈子能備極榆揚末復進一心之論尤見忠悃
帝王所以敷鬯聲教恢擴弘猷躋熙皡之
休揚乂安之烈者非徒著飾夫文具而取
辦于武功已也要必有至聖之德篤于淵
微至神之幾妙于獨運故其存之也玄遠
===
而不可測其發之也時出而不可窺以化
成天下也而聲教曁于四方以肅將天威
也而弘猷奠於萬世夫是以綏懷戢寧遠
至邇安而帝業以成治道無疆也於戲此
天道也天之道於穆不已者也化工默運
而溫冽之氣通復之序萬物生且成乎其
間矣帝王之道則天者也至德無爲而仁
義之用恩威之布天下和且平於其間矣
是故帝王之文非以致飾於天下也治定
punctuated:
國家文武一道，威德兼隆，信足以軼唐虞而媲成周者。子能鋪張惕厲，以鳴其盛，而純一不息之論，更覘臣子忠愛無已之情，宜錄以式。

考試官教授王批：「我皇上嗣統，覲揚光烈，子能備極榆揚，末復進一心之論，尤見忠悃。」

帝王所以敷鬯聲教、恢擴弘猷、躋熙皡之休、揚乂安之烈者，非徒著飾夫文具而取辦于武功已也。要必有至聖之德篤于淵微，至神之幾妙于獨運，故其存之也玄遠而不可測，其發之也時出而不可窺。以化成天下也，而聲教曁于四方；以肅將天威也，而弘猷奠於萬世。夫是以綏懷戢寧，遠至邇安，而帝業以成，治道無疆也。於戲！此天道也。天之道，於穆不已者也。化工默運，而溫冽之氣、通復之序，萬物生且成乎其間矣。帝王之道，則天者也。至德無爲，而仁義之用、恩威之布，天下和且平於其間矣。是故帝王之文，非以致飾於天下也。治定
translation_en:
In our state, civil and military governance form a single Way, and imperial might and virtue flourish together. It truly surpasses the ages of Tang and Yu and matches the perfected Zhou. You have elaborated upon this and urged vigilance, proclaiming its greatness. Your discussion of undivided, unceasing commitment further reveals a subject’s inexhaustible loyalty and devotion. It merits inclusion as a model.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Professor: “Our emperor has succeeded to the imperial line and gloriously proclaimed its illustrious achievements [?]. You have praised these to the fullest [?], and at the end further advanced an argument for singleness of mind, especially revealing your heartfelt loyalty.”

The means by which emperors and kings spread their civilizing influence and instruction, extend their grand designs, attain the blessings of radiant peace, and proclaim the achievements of orderly government are not merely the embellishment of ceremonial forms and reliance upon military accomplishments. They must possess the virtue of supreme sagehood, firmly rooted in the profound and subtle, and a supremely numinous capacity to discern incipient changes, wondrous in its independent operation. Thus, when held within, it is mysterious, far-reaching, and unfathomable; when manifested, it emerges at the appropriate time, and its workings cannot be discerned. Through transforming and perfecting all under Heaven, their civilizing influence and instruction reach the four quarters; through reverently carrying forth Heaven’s might, their grand designs are established for ten thousand generations. In this way they bring reassurance and allegiance, restraint and tranquillity: those far away come to them, those nearby are secure, imperial achievement is accomplished, and the Way of governance has no bounds. Ah! This is the Way of Heaven.

The Way of Heaven is profound and unceasing. Its transforming work proceeds silently; amid the vital forces of warmth and cold and the ordered succession of circulation and return, the myriad things are born and brought to maturity. The Way of emperors and kings takes Heaven as its model. Supreme virtue acts without contrivance; through the exercise of benevolence and righteousness and the distribution of favor and authority, all under Heaven becomes harmonious and peaceful. Thus, the civil accomplishments of emperors and kings do not serve merely to embellish all under Heaven. When order is established…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
而文斯顯則天下以文賛之其諸天道陽
舒之運而能培國家元氣之長者乎帝王
之武非以立威於天下也亂輯而武斯顯
則天下以武賛之其諸天道陰肅之運而
能揚國家神氣之精者乎故唐堯之大也
書稱之則曰乃武乃文夫堯起諸侯而爲
天子光天下是文武之放勳也然惟帝德
廣運爾堯不自知也周文之盛也詩稱之
則曰文武維后夫文王起岐周而爲西伯
===
顯西土是文武之顯謨也然惟厥德不回
爾文亦不自知也武王之順天應人燮伐
大商武功成焉遂訪箕子敘九疇皇極敷
言之訓而至文于是乎闡矣周公之繼武
相成卜建東都武功寓焉乃作洛誥訓殷
頑畢公保釐之命而文教于是乎著矣至
于宣王紹文武之績成安攘之勳會諸侯
于東都復有周之境土詩人於車攻美其
簡閱焉於吉日美其蒐獮焉蓋兵戢而時
punctuated: 而文斯顯，則天下以文賛之，其諸天道陽舒之運，而能培國家元氣之長者乎？帝王之武，非以立威於天下也。亂輯而武斯顯，則天下以武賛之，其諸天道陰肅之運，而能揚國家神氣之精者乎？故唐堯之大也，書稱之則曰：「乃武乃文。」夫堯起諸侯而爲天子，光天下，是文武之放勳也。然惟帝德廣運爾，堯不自知也。周文之盛也，詩稱之則曰：「文武維后。」夫文王起岐周而爲西伯，顯西土，是文武之顯謨也。然惟厥德不回爾，文亦不自知也。武王之順天應人，燮伐大商，武功成焉，遂訪箕子，敘九疇、皇極敷言之訓，而至文于是乎闡矣。周公之繼武相成，卜建東都，武功寓焉，乃作《洛誥》，訓殷頑，畢公保釐之命，而文教于是乎著矣。至于宣王紹文武之績，成安攘之勳，會諸侯于東都，復有周之境土，詩人於《車攻》美其簡閱焉，於《吉日》美其蒐獮焉，蓋兵戢而時
translation_en:
…and civil virtue thereby becomes manifest, then all under Heaven praise them for it. Is this not like the expansive working of Heaven’s yang, nurturing the growth of the state’s primal vitality? The martial prowess of emperors and kings is not intended merely to establish their authority over all under Heaven. When disorder has been quelled and martial prowess thereby becomes manifest, all under Heaven praise them for it. Is this not like the stern working of Heaven’s yin, bringing forth the concentrated spiritual vigor of the state?

Thus, of the greatness of Tang Yao, the Book of Documents says: “Both martial and civil.” Yao rose from among the feudal lords to become the Son of Heaven and illumined all under Heaven: this was his far-reaching achievement in both civil and martial affairs. Yet it was simply that his imperial virtue extended widely; Yao himself was unaware of it. Of the flourishing virtue of King Wen of Zhou, the Book of Odes says: “Civil and martial is the sovereign.” King Wen rose in Qizhou to become the Lord of the West and brought glory to the western lands: this was his illustrious design in both civil and martial affairs. Yet it was simply that his virtue did not deviate; Wen, too, was unaware of it.

King Wu followed Heaven and responded to the people, joining forces to attack Great Shang and accomplishing his martial achievement. He then consulted Jizi, setting forth the Nine Categories and the teachings on the Sovereign’s Ultimate Standard and the promulgation of its words; thus the highest civil virtue was made manifest. The Duke of Zhou carried on King Wu’s work and assisted King Cheng, using divination to establish the eastern capital; martial achievement was embodied in this. He then composed the “Announcement concerning Luo” to instruct the recalcitrant people of Yin; there was also the charge to the Duke of Bi to preserve order and govern, and civil instruction thereby became evident.

As for King Xuan, he continued the achievements of Kings Wen and Wu, accomplishing the work of securing peace within and repelling threats from without. He assembled the feudal lords at the eastern capital and recovered Zhou’s territory. In “Our Chariots Were Strong,” the poet praised his inspections and reviews; in “The Auspicious Day,” the poet praised his spring and autumn hunts. For arms are laid aside, yet at the proper time…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
動動則威備弛則玩玩則無振此宣王之
用文事而飭武功所以爲內順治而外威
嚴也夫文武之用與變推移而張弛之機
隨時以著周之盛王所以爲聖而至今傳
頌之不衰者也洪惟我
太祖高皇帝之開天也混一區宇汛掃腥羶武
功亢矣是故其平江漢也翦吳會也討蜀
越也戡荆湖也以及于元都廓清西南底
定開闢之極功也夷考其渡江
===
登極之詔所謂克當天心受天明命者與然而
簡命儒臣集禮典樂釐正
郊祀升中因吉立臥碑於黌宮也頒
大誥於中外也蓋六合嚮德而遠邇同文矣方
天心厭亂神異潜孚若有以默發
聖心焉一仗劔而羣雄懾服九有頌聲是啓億
萬載之耿光者與帝堯同運非富天下者
也
成祖文皇帝之繼天也起自北平嗣大
punctuated:
動，動則威，備弛則玩，玩則無振。此宣王之用文事而飭武功，所以爲內順治而外威嚴也。夫文武之用，與變推移，而張弛之機，隨時以著。周之盛王所以爲聖，而至今傳頌之不衰者也。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝之開天也，混一區宇，汛掃腥羶，武功亢矣。是故其平江漢也，翦吳會也，討蜀越也，戡荆湖也，以及于元都廓清，西南底定，開闢之極功也。夷考其渡江登極之詔，所謂克當天心、受天明命者與？然而簡命儒臣，集禮典樂，釐正郊祀，升中因吉，立臥碑於黌宮也，頒大誥於中外也，蓋六合嚮德而遠邇同文矣。方天心厭亂，神異潜孚，若有以默發聖心焉。一仗劔而羣雄懾服，九有頌聲，是啓億萬載之耿光者，與帝堯同運，非富天下者也。
成祖文皇帝之繼天也，起自北平，嗣大
translation_en:
…acted when the time required. Action inspired awe; slackened preparations bred negligence, and negligence left them unable to rouse themselves. This was how King Xuan employed civil affairs and put military achievements in order, securing orderly government within and imposing authority abroad. The application of civil and military measures shifts with changing circumstances, while the occasions for tightening and relaxing become apparent as the times demand. This is what made the flourishing kings of Zhou sages, whose praises continue undiminished to this day.
We reverently reflect upon how our Emperor Taizu Gao inaugurated the dynasty: he united the realm and swept away the rank and fetid presence of alien rule. His military achievements were supreme. His pacification of Jianghan, destruction of the forces in Wuhui, campaigns against Shu and Yue, and subjugation of Jinghu, culminating in the clearing of the Yuan capital and the settlement of the southwest, were the highest achievements of a dynastic founding. Examining his edicts on crossing the Yangzi and ascending the throne, do we not find what is meant by answering Heaven’s will and receiving Heaven’s luminous mandate? Yet he also selected and appointed Confucian ministers, compiled rites and regulated music, rectified the suburban sacrifices, and reported his accomplishments to Heaven on an auspicious occasion [?]. He erected recumbent steles in the schools and promulgated the Grand Pronouncements throughout the capital and the provinces. Thus all within the six directions turned toward his virtue, and places far and near shared a common culture. At that time, Heaven’s heart abhorred disorder, and wondrous signs offered hidden confirmation, as though silently awakening his sagely mind. Once he took up the sword, the contending heroes submitted in fear, and songs of praise filled the nine regions. In inaugurating a resplendent glory that would endure for countless ages, he shared the enterprise of Emperor Yao; he did not regard possession of all under Heaven as his personal wealth.
When Emperor Chengzu Wen succeeded to Heaven’s mandate, he rose from Beiping and inherited the great …

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
歷服武烈彰矣是故其戡寧夏也降西戎也
掃幕北也克南交也以至于島夷歸命遼
海靜波皆丕承之偉績也夷考其定鼎金
陵之
詔所謂克相上帝寵綏四方者與然而肇創內
閣崇重儒臣日
御經筵不廢寒暑廣脩纂以訂書籍也
頒大全以訓諸士也蓋臣民仰德而治教休
明矣方
===
天命有在祥異荐徵若有默定大數焉一揮戈
而內難悉平四方頌德是弘億萬載之大
烈者與文武同道不失天下之顯名者也
迨我
世宗肅皇帝之入承
大統也則發明正學而
敬一著箴也闡揚儒術而
五箴釋註也
重幸胄監而
punctuated:
歷服，武烈彰矣。是故其戡寧夏也，降西戎也，掃幕北也，克南交也，以至于島夷歸命，遼海靜波，皆丕承之偉績也。夷考其定鼎金陵之詔，所謂克相上帝、寵綏四方者與？然而肇創內閣，崇重儒臣，日御經筵，不廢寒暑；廣脩纂以訂書籍也，頒大全以訓諸士也。蓋臣民仰德，而治教休明矣。方天命有在，祥異荐徵，若有默定大數焉。一揮戈而內難悉平，四方頌德，是弘億萬載之大烈者，與文武同道，不失天下之顯名者也。
迨我世宗肅皇帝之入承大統也，則發明正學而《敬一》著箴也，闡揚儒術而《五箴》釋註也，重幸胄監而
translation_en:
…the imperial succession, and his martial achievements shone forth. Thus his pacification of Ningxia, his subjugation of the western Rong, his sweeping campaigns north of the desert, and his conquest of southern Jiaozhi—even the submission of the island peoples and the stilling of the waves of the Liaohai—all were great achievements in carrying forward his inheritance. Examining closely his edict establishing the capital at Jinling, was this not what it meant by “ably assisting the Lord on High and graciously pacifying the four quarters”? Yet he also founded the Grand Secretariat, honored Confucian ministers, and attended the Classics Colloquium daily, without interruption in cold or heat. He sponsored extensive compilation to establish authoritative texts and promulgated the Complete Compendia to instruct scholars. His subjects looked up to his virtue, and government and moral instruction were splendid and enlightened. At that time, Heaven’s mandate rested with him, and auspicious marvels repeatedly supplied confirmation, as though something had silently settled the great course of destiny. With one sweep of his halberd, all internal troubles were quelled, and the four quarters praised his virtue. Thus he extended his great achievements for countless ages, following the same Way as Kings Wen and Wu and preserving his illustrious name throughout the realm.
When our Emperor Shizong, posthumously styled Su, came to inherit the imperial succession, he elucidated orthodox learning by composing the Admonition on Reverent Unity, and promoted Confucian teachings by providing explanatory annotations to the Five Admonitions. He again visited the Directorate of Education, and …

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
郊祀之親俯採禮官之議
幸學之典益隆重道之儀
御經筵則儒臣進講以資啓沃也重科目則表
正文體以挽淳風也皆
聖政之要務是天下之至文也如邊圉少警有
諭誡之辭儲積未充有實邊之
令以六師未振非所以重武衛也
親大閱以激勵之邊才未廣非所以重封疆
也
===
命諸司得薦揚之是詰戎訓武之規卽
祖宗之遺也
聖猷神斷淵乎弘深中外諸臣欣逢快覩仰窺
我
皇上文武之德固將鬯
聲敎於無外壯
皇猷於無疆者其與隆古盛王先後一道授受
一心猶天之造化生成乎萬物溫冽爲序
通復相成而不自知也草茅之所欲竊有
punctuated:
郊祀之親，俯採禮官之議；幸學之典，益隆重道之儀。御經筵，則儒臣進講以資啓沃也；重科目，則表正文體以挽淳風也。皆聖政之要務，是天下之至文也。如邊圉少警，有諭誡之辭；儲積未充，有實邊之令。以六師未振，非所以重武衛也，親大閱以激勵之；邊才未廣，非所以重封疆也，命諸司得薦揚之。是詰戎訓武之規，卽祖宗之遺也。
聖猷神斷，淵乎弘深！中外諸臣欣逢快覩，仰窺我皇上文武之德，固將鬯聲敎於無外，壯皇猷於無疆者。其與隆古盛王先後一道，授受一心，猶天之造化生成乎萬物，溫冽爲序，通復相成，而不自知也。草茅之所欲竊有
translation_en:
… In personally performing the suburban sacrifices, he graciously heeds the deliberations of the ritual officials; through the ceremony of visiting the Imperial University, he further dignifies the observances honoring the Way. When he attends the Classics Colloquium, Confucian officials deliver lectures to nourish his understanding; in attaching importance to the examinations, he sets literary composition right, restoring an uncorrupted ethos. These are all essential tasks of sagely government, the highest expressions of civil refinement under Heaven. When even a slight alarm arises on the frontier, he issues admonitory instructions; when provisions are insufficient, he commands that the frontier be supplied. Considering that the Six Armies’ lack of vigor fails to give due weight to military defense, he personally conducts a grand review to spur them on. Considering that the limited pool of frontier talent fails to give due weight to the defense of the realm, he authorizes the various offices to recommend and advance such men. These measures for ordering the troops and training them in warfare are precisely the legacy of the imperial ancestors.
How profound and far-reaching are his sagely plans and inspired decisions! Officials at court and in the provinces rejoice to encounter and behold them. Looking reverently upon Our Emperor’s civil and martial virtues, they see that he will surely extend his civilizing influence everywhere and magnify his imperial achievements without limit. He and the illustrious kings of high antiquity, though living in different ages, follow a single Way, transmitting and receiving it with one mind. It is like Heaven’s creative transformation, which brings the myriad things into being and nurtures them to maturity: warmth and cold follow in order, unfolding and return complete one another, without conscious awareness. As for what this humble rustic would venture to offer …

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
獻者無亦以
天道望我
皇上而已上天之運不息而其化有漸生物不
測者其功也而為物不二者其本也故天
道不二而
聖心惟一一則純純則無欲一則恒恒則無息
思
天之民不可下也懷保之政常先焉思
天之臣不可易也激勸之典常隆焉思
===
天之權不可褻也近習之馭常嚴焉思
天之明不可息也經筵之講常重焉順
天命者必揚違
天道者必絀所以培元氣於靈長振神氣於赫
奕者率不外此是道也即
祖宗之道而堯文武宣之所以為文武者統是
矣書曰惟天聰明惟聖時憲愚願以為吾
君告不識可以轉聞于
上否
punctuated:
獻者，無亦以天道望我皇上而已。上天之運不息，而其化有漸。生物不測者，其功也；而為物不二者，其本也。故天道不二，而聖心惟一。一則純，純則無欲；一則恒，恒則無息。
思天之民不可下也，懷保之政常先焉；思天之臣不可易也，激勸之典常隆焉；思天之權不可褻也，近習之馭常嚴焉；思天之明不可息也，經筵之講常重焉。順天命者必揚，違天道者必絀。所以培元氣於靈長、振神氣於赫奕者，率不外此。是道也，即祖宗之道，而堯文武宣之所以為文武者，統是矣。《書》曰：「惟天聰明，惟聖時憲。」愚願以為吾君告，不識可以轉聞于上否？
translation_en:
…to offer is perhaps merely the hope that our Emperor will take the Way of Heaven as his standard. Heaven’s movement never ceases, yet its transforming influence proceeds gradually. Bringing forth living things in unfathomable ways is its achievement; remaining undivided in its making of things is its foundation. Thus the Way of Heaven is undivided, and the sagely mind is single. Singleness brings purity, and purity brings freedom from desire; singleness brings constancy, and constancy brings unceasing activity.
Reflect that Heaven’s people must not be treated as lowly: policies that cherish and protect them must always come first. Reflect that Heaven’s ministers must not be treated lightly: measures to inspire and encourage them must always be generously upheld. Reflect that Heaven’s authority must not be profaned: close attendants must always be strictly controlled. Reflect that Heaven’s illumination must not cease: lectures at the Classics Colloquium must always receive due weight. Those who follow Heaven’s mandate must be promoted; those who violate Heaven’s Way must be dismissed. The means of nourishing the primal vital force so that it endures, and rousing the spiritual energy to radiant vigor, lie entirely within these principles. This Way is precisely the Way of the imperial ancestors; it also encompasses that through which Yao, Wen, Wu, and Xuan achieved their civil and martial excellence [?]. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven alone is discerning; the sage alone takes it as his model.” In my humble judgment, I wish to offer this as counsel to our ruler. Might it be conveyed to His Majesty?

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
第二問
洪敷誥
同考試官教諭梁批聖賢道統之傳發明詳盡而
末總歸之天尤為有見于其潛心斯道而有得者與
考試官教諭陳批知道之言出人意表
考試官教授王批諸說異同剖析獨為明盡
斯道之在天下也有相承之統君子固當
沿其源而遡其流古人之尚論也有不一
之見學者不可執其疑而失其是夫道之
===
有統也前乎千百世之上以承天道而主
斯文後乎千百世之下以繼往聖而興來
學然時有顯晦而道無存亡言有詳略而
聖無加損君子惟當觀其大旨究其意之
所存焉爾豈可據其一而疑之哉今夫道
統之說何所昉乎董子曰道之大原出于
天是天者道統之所自來也傳曰聖人者
道之管是聖人者道統之所由寄也粵自
洪荒以上記載無傳故孔子敘書斷自唐
punctuated:
第二問
洪敷誥
同考試官教諭梁批：聖賢道統之傳，發明詳盡，而末總歸之天，尤為有見。于其潛心斯道而有得者與？
考試官教諭陳批：知道之言，出人意表。
考試官教授王批：諸說異同，剖析獨為明盡。
斯道之在天下也，有相承之統，君子固當沿其源而遡其流。古人之尚論也，有不一之見，學者不可執其疑而失其是。夫道之有統也，前乎千百世之上，以承天道而主斯文；後乎千百世之下，以繼往聖而興來學。然時有顯晦，而道無存亡；言有詳略，而聖無加損。君子惟當觀其大旨，究其意之所存焉爾，豈可據其一而疑之哉？今夫道統之說，何所昉乎？董子曰：「道之大原出于天。」是天者，道統之所自來也。傳曰：「聖人者，道之管。」是聖人者，道統之所由寄也。粵自洪荒以上，記載無傳，故孔子敘書，斷自唐
translation_en:
Second Question
Hong Fugao

Comment by Associate Examiner Liang, Instructor: “The transmission of the succession of the Way through the sages and worthies is elucidated thoroughly and fully. The final attribution of it all to Heaven is especially insightful. Might he be someone who has devoted himself to this Way and attained an understanding of it [?]?”

Comment by Examiner Chen, Instructor: “These words reveal an understanding of the Way and go beyond what one would expect.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Professor: “The analysis of the similarities and differences among the various explanations is exceptionally clear and thorough.”

This Way, as it exists in the world, has a continuous line of transmission. The gentleman should indeed follow its source and trace its current upstream. In appraising the ancients, opinions differ; students must not cling to what is doubtful and thereby lose sight of what is correct. As for the succession of the Way, those who stood a thousand or a hundred generations before us received the Way of Heaven and presided over this cultural tradition; those who stand a thousand or a hundred generations afterward carry on the sages of the past and inspire the learners to come. Yet although there are times of prominence and obscurity, the Way neither comes into being nor perishes. Although statements may be detailed or brief, the sageliness of the sages is neither increased nor diminished. The gentleman should simply observe their broad purport and investigate where their intent lies. How could one seize upon a single point and on that basis cast doubt upon them?

Now, where did the account of the succession of the Way originate? Master Dong said: “The great source of the Way comes from Heaven.” Thus Heaven is that from which the succession of the Way derives. A transmitted text says: “The sage is the conduit of the Way.” Thus the sage is the one in whom the succession of the Way is lodged. No written records have survived from the primordial age or earlier. Therefore, when Confucius arranged the Book of Documents, he set its starting point at Tang…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
虞者以精一之旨自堯而始也然三代以
上其統每屬之在位之人若堯舜之後有
禹湯禹湯之後有文武文武之後有周公
爲君爲相位各不同要皆達而在上其道
行行者統之所由立也三代以下其統每
屬之無位之士若孔子之後有孟軻孟軻
之後有周程朱子或師或友時各未遇要
皆窮而在下其道明明者統之所由紹也
此其大槩也試舉孟子終篇之疑韓愈原
===
道之論及孔門宋儒之緒而悉論之彼自
精一執中承堯之統者舜也原道謂堯以
是傳之舜矣孟子乃以堯舜至湯一舉而
並言之何也蓋孟子謂斯道大約五百年
而一興故凡肇統于先者均啓嗣聖之緒
初無彼此也非軼舜也視韓所述何有于
軒輊乎祗台德先承舜之統者禹也原道
謂舜以是傳之禹矣孟子乃以禹皐陶爲
見知而不敘諸統何也蓋孟子惟以五百
punctuated:
虞者，以精一之旨自堯而始也。然三代以上，其統每屬之在位之人。若堯舜之後有禹湯，禹湯之後有文武，文武之後有周公，爲君爲相，位各不同，要皆達而在上，其道行；行者，統之所由立也。三代以下，其統每屬之無位之士。若孔子之後有孟軻，孟軻之後有周程朱子，或師或友，時各未遇，要皆窮而在下，其道明；明者，統之所由紹也。此其大槩也。試舉孟子終篇之疑、韓愈《原道》之論及孔門宋儒之緒而悉論之。
彼自精一執中，承堯之統者，舜也。《原道》謂堯以是傳之舜矣，孟子乃以堯舜至湯一舉而並言之，何也？蓋孟子謂斯道大約五百年而一興，故凡肇統于先者，均啓嗣聖之緒，初無彼此也，非軼舜也。視韓所述，何有于軒輊乎？祗台德先，承舜之統者，禹也。《原道》謂舜以是傳之禹矣，孟子乃以禹皐陶爲見知而不敘諸統，何也？蓋孟子惟以五百
translation_en:
…and Yu: this was because the purport of being discerning and single-minded began with Yao. During the Three Dynasties and earlier, however, the succession to the Way generally belonged to men holding office. Thus, after Yao and Shun came Yu and Tang; after Yu and Tang came Wen and Wu; and after Wen and Wu came the Duke of Zhou. Whether rulers or ministers, their positions differed, but all attained prominence and occupied high stations, so that their Way was put into practice. It was through its practice that the succession was established. After the Three Dynasties, the succession generally belonged to scholars without office. Thus, after Confucius came Meng Ke; after Meng Ke came the masters Zhou, Cheng, and Zhu. Whether teachers or friends, none found an opportunity suited to his time; all remained in straitened circumstances and lowly stations, yet their Way was elucidated. It was through this elucidation that the succession was continued. Such is the broad outline. Let us take up the doubts raised by the final chapter of the Mencius, Han Yu’s arguments in Inquiry into the Way, and the continuing tradition of the Confucian school and the Song scholars, and discuss them fully.
It was Shun who, through discernment and single-mindedness and holding fast to the Mean, inherited Yao’s succession. Inquiry into the Way says that Yao transmitted this to Shun. Yet Mencius speaks of Yao and Shun together in a single statement about the period from them to Tang. Why? Mencius held that this Way flourished anew approximately once every five hundred years. Thus, all those who first established the succession equally opened the tradition for the sages who followed; he made no distinction between them. He did not pass over Shun. Compared with Han Yu’s account, how could there be any question of superiority or inferiority? It was Yu who, “reverently putting my virtue first” [?], inherited Shun’s succession. Inquiry into the Way says that Shun transmitted this to Yu. Yet Mencius classifies Yu and Gao Yao as those who knew the Way through seeing it, without including them in his account of the succession. Why? Because Mencius took five hundred…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
年爲斯道一傳故凡未越百年者均屬見
知之列原無優劣也非略禹也視韓所敘
何有于低昂乎當殷士之來歸親訪洪範
之傳使斯道旣蔽而復明者文之後賴有
武王也而孟氏終篇無一言及之若于武
爲未與于統者然不知父子迭聖同出一
時稱人世德從其所尊玆敘文而不及武
者豈非以舉父則子可該之意歟觀其他
日敘統于文王之後復繼以不泄不忘之
===
言則可以知孟子敘武之心矣原道所謂
湯以是傳之文武者不旣同耶當周命之
方新大衍禮樂之制親覩文考之懿範者
見知莫周公若也孟子乃置之不言而顧
及于宜生之儔若以周公爲無得于文王
者然不知交儆以道祗在君臣信史之傳
取其協贊玆周公之不與于見知者豈非
以父子之間而略之歟觀其他日敘統于
武王之後復綴之思兼數語則可以諒孟
punctuated:
年爲斯道一傳，故凡未越百年者，均屬見知之列，原無優劣也，非略禹也。視韓所敘，何有于低昂乎？
當殷士之來歸，親訪《洪範》之傳，使斯道旣蔽而復明者，文之後賴有武王也。而孟氏終篇無一言及之，若于武爲未與于統者然。不知父子迭聖，同出一時，稱人世德，從其所尊。玆敘文而不及武者，豈非以舉父則子可該之意歟？觀其他日敘統于文王之後，復繼以「不泄不忘」之言，則可以知孟子敘武之心矣。《原道》所謂「湯以是傳之文武」者，不旣同耶？
當周命之方新，大衍禮樂之制，親覩文考之懿範者，見知莫周公若也。孟子乃置之不言，而顧及于宜生之儔，若以周公爲無得于文王者然。不知交儆以道，祗在君臣；信史之傳，取其協贊。玆周公之不與于見知者，豈非以父子之間而略之歟？觀其他日敘統于武王之後，復綴之「思兼」數語，則可以諒孟
translation_en:
…years as the interval between transmissions of this Way. Thus all those separated by no more than a hundred years belong among those who knew it through direct observation. There was originally no distinction of superiority or inferiority: this was no slight to Yu. Compared with Han Yu’s account, what difference in standing is there?
When the officers of Yin came over in allegiance, it was King Wu, following King Wen, upon whom they relied to inquire personally into the transmission of the Great Plan (Hongfan), and to bring this Way back to light after it had been obscured. Yet throughout his final chapter Mengzi makes no mention of him, as though King Wu had no part in the succession of the Way. This overlooks the fact that father and son were sages in succession, appearing in the same age; in praising a family’s hereditary virtue, one follows its most honored member. In recounting King Wen here without mentioning King Wu, was the intention not that naming the father could also encompass the son? Elsewhere, when Mengzi recounts the succession after King Wen, he continues with the words “neither slackening nor forgetting.” From this we can understand his intention in treating King Wu. Is this not the same as the statement in On the Way (Yuandao), “Tang transmitted this to Wen and Wu”?
When Zhou’s mandate was newly established and the institutions of rites and music were greatly elaborated, no one equaled the Duke of Zhou in knowing the Way through direct observation, having personally witnessed the admirable example of his illustrious deceased father. Yet Mengzi passes him over in silence and instead mentions the likes of Yisheng, as though the Duke of Zhou had gained nothing from King Wen. This overlooks the fact that mutual admonition through the Way pertains specifically to ruler and minister; what trustworthy historical accounts record is their cooperative assistance. Is the Duke of Zhou’s omission here from those who knew through direct observation not due to passing over the relationship between father and son? Elsewhere, when Mengzi recounts the succession after King Wu, he appends several phrases beginning “he thought to combine.” From this we can understand Mengzi’s…

年爲斯道一傳故凡未越百年者均屬見
知之列原無優劣也非略禹也視韓所敘
何有于低昂乎當殷士之來歸親訪洪範

translation_en:
…years constitute one transmission of this Way. Thus all those separated by no more than a hundred years belong among those who knew it through personal observation. There was originally no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor was Yu slighted. Compared with Han Yu’s account, how is anyone exalted or diminished? When the men of Yin came over in allegiance, it was King Wu who personally inquired into the transmission of the Great Plan. That this Way, having fallen into decay, shone forth again after King Wen was thanks to King Wu. Yet throughout his chapter Mengzi says not a word about him, seemingly treating King Wu as having no part in the succession of the Way. This overlooks the fact that father and son were successive sages who appeared in the same age: in praising a family’s virtue across generations, one follows its most honored member. Does mentioning King Wen here without mentioning King Wu not mean that naming the father also includes the son? Elsewhere, when Mengzi recounts the succession after King Wen, he follows it with the words “neither remiss nor forgetful.” From this we can understand his intention in treating King Wu. This overlooks the fact that mutual admonition through the Way pertains specifically to ruler and minister, and that the reliable historical account selects those who assisted in its advancement. Is the Duke of Zhou’s exclusion here from those who knew through personal observation not because he was passed over on account of the father–son relationship? Elsewhere, when Mengzi recounts the succession after King Wu, he adds a few words about “thinking to combine” their achievements. From this we can understand Meng…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
子敘周公之心矣原道所謂文武以是傳
之周公者不旣合耶要之禹之去堯舜也
武周之去文王也皆在百年之內故禹為
見知非有所劣武周之不得嗣統于文王
非有所遺也由堯舜至湯也由湯至文王
也由文王至孔子也適當乎五百之期故
湯文雖非有加于禹而得以直接乎虞夏
孔子雖非賢於周公而得以直接乎文王
也昔草廬謂伏羲為上古之元堯舜其亨
===
禹湯其利文武周公其貞非有見而云然
乎愚謂道統之所由立者蓋如此自周轍
旣東大道日隱文武周公之緒幾墜于地
矣惟夫子講道于洙泗之濱而一貫之旨
為萬世傳心之脉于時及門之士蓋三千
而得其宗者獨顏氏曾氏也然後世敘統
反不及焉豈非以聖師在上門弟不得以
亢其軌歟自列國爭雄權謀相煽孔門仁
義一脉幾于漸絕矣惟孟子壁立于羣雄
punctuated:
子敘周公之心矣。《原道》所謂文武以是傳之周公者，不旣合耶？要之，禹之去堯舜也，武周之去文王也，皆在百年之內，故禹為見知，非有所劣；武周之不得嗣統于文王，非有所遺也。由堯舜至湯也，由湯至文王也，由文王至孔子也，適當乎五百之期，故湯文雖非有加于禹，而得以直接乎虞夏；孔子雖非賢於周公，而得以直接乎文王也。昔草廬謂伏羲為上古之元，堯舜其亨，禹湯其利，文武周公其貞，非有見而云然乎？愚謂道統之所由立者，蓋如此。
自周轍旣東，大道日隱，文武周公之緒幾墜于地矣。惟夫子講道于洙泗之濱，而一貫之旨為萬世傳心之脉。于時及門之士蓋三千，而得其宗者獨顏氏曾氏也。然後世敘統反不及焉，豈非以聖師在上，門弟不得以亢其軌歟？自列國爭雄，權謀相煽，孔門仁義一脉幾于漸絕矣。惟孟子壁立于羣雄
translation_en:
…the intention behind Mengzi’s account of the Duke of Zhou can thus be understood. Does this not accord with the statement in “An Inquiry into the Way” (Yuan dao) that Kings Wen and Wu transmitted this Way to the Duke of Zhou? In essence, Yu lived within a hundred years of Yao and Shun, as did King Wu and the Duke of Zhou of King Wen. Thus, Yu’s knowing the Way through direct observation implies no inferiority; nor does the absence of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou as successors to King Wen in the lineage imply any omission. From Yao and Shun to Tang, from Tang to King Wen, and from King Wen to Kongzi, the intervals corresponded precisely to periods of five hundred years. Hence Tang and King Wen, though not superior to Yu, could succeed directly to the legacy of Yu and Xia; Kongzi, though not more worthy than the Duke of Zhou, could succeed directly to King Wen. Caolu once said that Fuxi represented the “origination” of high antiquity, Yao and Shun its “flourishing,” Yu and Tang its “benefit,” and Kings Wen and Wu and the Duke of Zhou its “constancy.” Surely he spoke thus from insight? In my humble view, this is how the lineage of the Way came to be established.
After the Zhou royal chariots moved east, the Great Way grew more obscure by the day, and the legacy of Kings Wen and Wu and the Duke of Zhou nearly fell to the ground. It was the Master alone who expounded the Way on the banks of the Zhu and Si rivers, and his teaching of a single thread running through all became the enduring channel for transmitting the mind through ten thousand generations. At that time, some three thousand scholars entered his school, yet only Yan and Zeng grasped its essential meaning. Nevertheless, later accounts of the lineage omit them. Was this not because, with the sage teacher above them, his disciples could not stand on an equal footing with him? As the rival states contended for supremacy and inflamed one another with stratagems and intrigue, the single thread of benevolence and righteousness transmitted by Kongzi’s school came close to gradual extinction. Mengzi alone stood firm as a cliff amid the contending mighty…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
之中而知言養氣為吾道赤幟之立則聞
知孔子之道而繼其統者信無踰于孟氏
也然其自叙乃以見知自命豈其志在闢
邪以任之不親則排之不力歟濂溪周子
金井玉淵光風霽月圖書之作默契邃古
不傳之祕晦庵稱其非秦漢諸儒所及當
矣然伊川乃以孟子之後一人歸之明道
非無以也蓋伊川所稱祇以明道闢邪之
功可匹孟子非謂道統之傳輕濂溪為無
===
得也亦何妨于茂叔之統乎紫陽朱子苦
心極力繭絲牛毛著述之贍大發千聖之
奧許衡稱其集諸儒大成當矣然今為良
知之學者若于陸氏有取非無故也蓋陸
氏之學務明心朱子之學在窮理故恒情
樂徑悟而憚積累是以厭常而喜新也亦
何損于元晦之統乎要之孔子也顏曾孟
也倡斯道于大亂之後其任之也難此堯
舜湯文之道所以至今不廢也濂溪也程
punctuated:
之中，而知言養氣為吾道赤幟之立，則聞知孔子之道而繼其統者，信無踰于孟氏也。然其自叙乃以見知自命，豈其志在闢邪，以任之不親，則排之不力歟？濂溪周子，金井玉淵，光風霽月，圖書之作，默契邃古不傳之祕，晦庵稱其非秦漢諸儒所及，當矣。然伊川乃以孟子之後一人歸之明道，非無以也。蓋伊川所稱，祇以明道闢邪之功可匹孟子，非謂道統之傳，輕濂溪為無得也。亦何妨于茂叔之統乎？

紫陽朱子，苦心極力，繭絲牛毛，著述之贍，大發千聖之奧，許衡稱其集諸儒大成，當矣。然今為良知之學者，若于陸氏有取，非無故也。蓋陸氏之學務明心，朱子之學在窮理，故恒情樂徑悟而憚積累，是以厭常而喜新也。亦何損于元晦之統乎？

要之，孔子也，顏曾孟也，倡斯道于大亂之後，其任之也難，此堯舜湯文之道所以至今不廢也。濂溪也，程
translation_en:
…amid the contending powers, his understanding of words and cultivation of vital energy raised the crimson standard of our Way. Thus, among those who learned Confucius’s Way through hearing and succeeded to its transmission, surely none surpassed Mengzi. Yet in his own account he described himself as one who knew through direct encounter. Was this because his purpose lay in refuting heterodox teachings, and he believed that unless he took this responsibility personally, he could not oppose them forcefully?

Master Zhou of Lianxi, Zhou Dunyi, was like a golden well and a jade pool [?], like a clear breeze and the bright moon after rain. His diagram and writings silently accorded with the untransmitted mysteries of remote antiquity. Hui’an, Zhu Xi, rightly declared that the scholars of Qin and Han could not equal him. Yet Yichuan, Cheng Yi, had reason to accord Mingdao, Cheng Hao, the distinction of being the one man since Mengzi. Cheng Yi’s praise meant only that Cheng Hao’s achievement in refuting heterodox teachings could match Mengzi’s. It did not mean disparaging Zhou Dunyi as having gained nothing in the transmission of the Way. How, then, could it impair the place of Maoshu—Zhou Dunyi—in that transmission?

Master Zhu of Ziyang, Zhu Xi, labored painstakingly and exerted himself to the utmost. His abundant writings, as fine and numerous as silkworm threads and ox hairs, greatly illuminated the profound teachings of the myriad sages. Xu Heng rightly praised him for bringing the achievements of the various scholars to their fullest synthesis. Yet there is a reason why those now pursuing the learning of innate moral knowledge seem to find something to adopt in Master Lu’s teaching. Lu Jiuyuan’s learning strives to illuminate the mind, while Zhu Xi’s learning lies in investigating principle to the utmost. Ordinary human inclinations therefore favor direct awakening and shrink from gradual accumulation; hence people tire of the familiar and delight in the new. How could this diminish the place of Yuanhui—Zhu Xi—in the transmission?

In essence, Confucius, Yan Hui, Zengzi, and Mengzi championed this Way in the wake of great disorder; difficult indeed was the responsibility they bore. This is why the Way of Yao, Shun, Tang, and King Wen has not fallen into disuse even today. Zhou Dunyi of Lianxi, Cheng…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
朱也振絕學于寥廓之餘其見之也卓此
堯舜湯文之道所以千載一日也昔勉齋
謂由孔子而後曾子子思繼其微至孟子
而始著由孟子而後周程張子繼其微至
朱子而始著豈無見而妄言乎愚謂道統
之所由紹者蓋如此竊嘗論之道之傳與
不傳由于人之遇與不遇然有天焉非人
之所能與也不係于見聞之間吾嘗怪夫
孔門諸子若子貢者其悟非不敏其問非
===
不切也然終日侍于夫子之側乃謂性與
天道不可得而聞於戲文章之外豈復有
性與天道哉若回之愚參之魯則無不聞
矣何也蓋天之所與者在顏曾不在賜而
道之所傳者以遇不以見也故自古聖賢
以道相授受者其聞雖在于五百年之後
而其知則在于五百年之先由堯舜以下
逮于程朱皆遇也皆天也不然雖日侍其
側不可謂有所見雖日誦其書不可謂有
punctuated: 朱也，振絕學于寥廓之餘，其見之也卓，此堯舜湯文之道所以千載一日也。昔勉齋謂：「由孔子而後，曾子、子思繼其微，至孟子而始著；由孟子而後，周、程、張子繼其微，至朱子而始著。」豈無見而妄言乎？愚謂道統之所由紹者，蓋如此。竊嘗論之：道之傳與不傳，由于人之遇與不遇，然有天焉，非人之所能與也，不係于見聞之間。吾嘗怪夫孔門諸子，若子貢者，其悟非不敏，其問非不切也，然終日侍于夫子之側，乃謂性與天道不可得而聞。於戲！文章之外，豈復有性與天道哉？若回之愚、參之魯，則無不聞矣。何也？蓋天之所與者在顏、曾，不在賜，而道之所傳者以遇，不以見也。故自古聖賢以道相授受者，其聞雖在于五百年之後，而其知則在于五百年之先。由堯舜以下，逮于程朱，皆遇也，皆天也。不然，雖日侍其側，不可謂有所見；雖日誦其書，不可謂有
translation_en:
…and Zhu revived learning that had been cut off, after a vast interval of desolation. Their insight was outstanding: this is why the Way of Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wen remains the same across a thousand years as in a single day. Mianzhai once said: “After Kongzi, Zengzi and Zisi carried on its subtle transmission, which only with Mengzi became manifest. After Mengzi, Zhou, Cheng, and Master Zhang carried on its subtle transmission, which only with Master Zhu became manifest.” Could he have spoken rashly, without insight? In my humble view, this is how the succession of the Way has been continued.

I have ventured to consider this: whether the Way is transmitted depends upon whether people encounter one another; yet Heaven is at work here, and this is not something human effort can determine. It does not depend upon what one sees and hears. I have often wondered about disciples of Kongzi such as Zigong. His understanding was certainly quick, and his questions certainly searching. Yet, though he attended at the Master's side all day, he said that one could not obtain a hearing of the Master's teachings on human nature and the Way of Heaven. Alas! Beyond the Master's cultural teachings, could there be some separate human nature and Way of Heaven? Yet Hui, seemingly foolish, and Shen, seemingly dull, heard everything. Why was this? Because Heaven bestowed its gift upon Yan Hui and Zeng Shen, not upon Ci—that is, Zigong—and the transmission of the Way depended upon an encounter, not upon seeing.

Thus, among the sages and worthies of antiquity who passed the Way from one to another, although their hearing came five hundred years later, their understanding reached back to five hundred years before. From Yao and Shun down to Cheng and Zhu, all was a matter of such encounters; all was Heaven's doing. Otherwise, even if one attended at their side every day, one could not be said to have seen anything; even if one recited their writings every day, one could not be said to have…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
所聞而此心相遇之真知實有超于耳目
之所不及者矣嗟夫觀道統之絕續一係
于天是又世道升降之一大機也敢以質
于明問
第三問
秦延緒
同考試官教諭林批以經學守約爲言而考究
詳明議論精確予其博而能約者
考試官教諭陳批博雅之學精切之論錄之
===
考試官教授王批宏博淹貫之學於此作見之
文所以載道者也必持精約之論而後可
垂於無窮學所以明道者也必敦反約之
功而後有裨於實用何也道原於天管於
心匪文弗載匪學弗明也工著述者繁文
侈說而不求諸至當則其論畸焉而弗精
是裂乎道者也而奚以垂無窮之訓乎稽
往牒者遠綜博覽而不要其指歸則其功
泛焉而靡約是晦乎道者也而奚以裨身
punctuated:
所聞，而此心相遇之真知，實有超于耳目之所不及者矣。嗟夫！觀道統之絕續，一係于天，是又世道升降之一大機也。敢以質于明問。
第三問
秦延緒
同考試官教諭林批：以經學守約爲言，而考究詳明，議論精確，予其博而能約者。
考試官教諭陳批：博雅之學，精切之論，錄之。
考試官教授王批：宏博淹貫之學，於此作見之。
文所以載道者也，必持精約之論，而後可垂於無窮；學所以明道者也，必敦反約之功，而後有裨於實用。何也？道原於天，管於心，匪文弗載，匪學弗明也。工著述者，繁文侈說，而不求諸至當，則其論畸焉而弗精，是裂乎道者也，而奚以垂無窮之訓乎？稽往牒者，遠綜博覽，而不要其指歸，則其功泛焉而靡約，是晦乎道者也，而奚以裨身
translation_en:
…heard; yet the true understanding arising from the meeting of these hearts indeed transcends what ears and eyes can reach. Alas! The interruption or continuation of the transmission of the Way depends entirely upon Heaven. This is also a great pivot upon which the rise and decline of the world’s moral order turns. I venture to submit this for consideration in response to your discerning question.
Third Question
Qin Yanxu
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Instructor: He takes classical learning and adherence to essentials as his theme. His investigations are thorough and clear, and his arguments precise. I commend his ability to combine breadth with a grasp of essentials.
Comment by Examiner Chen, Instructor: Broad and refined learning, with penetrating and pertinent arguments. Selected.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Professor: This composition displays extensive, comprehensive, and thoroughly integrated learning.
Writing is the means of conveying the Way. Only when its arguments are exact and concise can it be handed down for all time. Learning is the means of illuminating the Way. Only when one earnestly cultivates the work of returning to essentials can it contribute to practical use. Why is this? The Way originates in Heaven and is governed within the heart [?]. Without writing it cannot be conveyed; without learning it cannot be illuminated. If those skilled in composition multiply ornate phrases and extravagant explanations without seeking what is perfectly fitting, their arguments become lopsided and lack precision. This fragments the Way: how could it furnish instruction to be handed down for all time? If those who investigate the records of the past range widely in their syntheses and reading without grasping their essential purport, their efforts become diffuse and lack focus. This obscures the Way: how could it benefit the person…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
心之實乎故善作者會其精而脩文則道
載於文而傳之也遠稽古者反其約以為
學則道明於學而積之也深究其歸則一
心盡之矣心存則道得文為至文學為實
學玆固多識者之要軌而儒生之所當亟
亟以講求者也今夫典籍何昉乎太古之
世其民醇醇其政悶悶上無誥戒之施下
安忘言之化時則人文未闡也粤自篆籀
形製載籍所以蔚興簡竹汗青文墨由是
===
駿發庖犧氏於是造書契以代結繩之政
焉羲黃以降洪荒載闢柬帙漸備三皇有
三墳以述大道之要五帝有五典以紀常
道之經是皆先天開人遐哉邈乎弗可尚
也已夏商以來風氣聿開制作廼作述八
索則八卦之奧義悉陳著九丘則九州之
風土具載是皆隨事立教因時有作殆弗
可加也已周人監于夏商方策大備外史
掌三皇五帝之書則國家之所職掌者此
punctuated:
心之實乎？故善作者會其精而脩文，則道載於文而傳之也遠；稽古者反其約以為學，則道明於學而積之也深。究其歸，則一心盡之矣。心存則道得，文為至文，學為實學。玆固多識者之要軌，而儒生之所當亟亟以講求者也。
今夫典籍何昉乎？太古之世，其民醇醇，其政悶悶，上無誥戒之施，下安忘言之化，時則人文未闡也。粤自篆籀形製，載籍所以蔚興，簡竹汗青，文墨由是駿發。庖犧氏於是造書契，以代結繩之政焉。羲黃以降，洪荒載闢，柬帙漸備。三皇有三墳，以述大道之要；五帝有五典，以紀常道之經。是皆先天開人，遐哉邈乎，弗可尚也已！夏商以來，風氣聿開，制作廼作。述八索，則八卦之奧義悉陳；著九丘，則九州之風土具載。是皆隨事立教，因時有作，殆弗可加也已！周人監于夏商，方策大備。外史掌三皇五帝之書，則國家之所職掌者此
translation_en:
…the practical cultivation of the mind? Thus, those skilled in composition bring together the essentials and refine their writing: the Way is thereby borne in writing and transmitted far into the future. Those who investigate antiquity return to its essentials in pursuing learning: the Way is thereby clarified through learning and deeply accumulated. Examining their ultimate destination, we find that the mind alone encompasses them all. When the mind is preserved, the Way is attained; writing becomes writing of the highest order, and learning becomes substantive learning. This is indeed the essential course for those of broad knowledge, and what Confucian scholars ought urgently to investigate.
Now, where did the canonical writings originate? In remotest antiquity, the people were simple and pure, and government was unobtrusive. Those above issued no admonitions or injunctions; those below rested content in a transforming influence that dispensed with words. At that time, human culture had not yet been unfolded. Once seal-script forms took shape, written records flourished; bamboo slips were dried to prepare them for writing, and literary composition developed vigorously. Paoxi thereupon created written signs to replace government by knotted cords. From Fuxi and Huangdi onward, the primordial wilderness was progressively opened up, and collections of writings gradually became complete. The Three Sovereigns had the Three Tombs (San fen), which set forth the essentials of the Great Way; the Five Emperors had the Five Canons (Wu dian), which recorded the enduring principles of the constant Way. All these anticipated Heaven and enlightened humanity [?]. How distant and remote they were—nothing could surpass them!
From the Xia and Shang onward, prevailing customs developed, and institutions and cultural works arose. The composition of the Eight Cords (Ba suo) fully set forth the profound meanings of the eight trigrams; the writing of the Nine Mounds (Jiu qiu) comprehensively recorded the customs and terrain of the Nine Provinces. All these established teachings in response to circumstances and produced writings suited to their times. There was scarcely anything that could be added to them! The people of Zhou took Xia and Shang as their models, and their written records became fully comprehensive. The Outer Scribe had charge of the writings of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; thus, what the state held in its official custody was this…

The people of Zhou took the Xia and Shang as their models, and written records became abundantly complete. The Outer Scribe had charge of the writings of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors; thus, what the state officially kept in its charge was this…

title: 隆慶四年廣西鄉試錄
text:
也楚左史倚相能讀三墳五典八索九丘
則學士大夫之所誦習者此也郁郁之文
六合同風九有共貫後有作者弗可及矣
逮乎叔季縟文勝而實德衰史籍繁而異
說熾仲尼懼覽者之不一也廼明舊章定
禮樂刪詩篇而為三百因魯史而脩春秋
讀易道以黜八索述職方以除九丘討論
墳典斷自唐虞皇姒以來之所著述多刪
而弗錄者豈其書盡無足采哉蓋世遠風
===
遐遺軌失據殘編斷簡贗說亂真故倡並
耕而治者藉說於神農述陰陽醫方者竊
談乎黃帝他如太素太初之論多涉謬悠
三皇十紀之書咸屬迂誕夫事無徵則聞
者創駭言有證則習者心融此仲尼所以
不能無所折衷也仲尼既歿聖學榛蕪戰
國從衡衆說蜂起挾藝者吐舌而爭談窮
經者分門而肄辯真偽溷淆莫可究詰於
是秦人乘之而坑焚之禍起矣斯豈可獨
punctuated: 也。楚左史倚相能讀《三墳》《五典》《八索》《九丘》，則學士大夫之所誦習者此也。郁郁之文，六合同風，九有共貫，後有作者弗可及矣。逮乎叔季，縟文勝而實德衰，史籍繁而異說熾。仲尼懼覽者之不一也，廼明舊章，定禮樂，刪詩篇而為三百，因魯史而脩《春秋》，讀易道以黜《八索》，述職方以除《九丘》，討論墳典，斷自唐虞。皇姒以來之所著述，多刪而弗錄者，豈其書盡無足采哉？蓋世遠風遐，遺軌失據，殘編斷簡，贗說亂真。故倡並耕而治者，藉說於神農；述陰陽醫方者，竊談乎黃帝。他如太素太初之論，多涉謬悠；三皇十紀之書，咸屬迂誕。夫事無徵，則聞者創駭；言有證，則習者心融。此仲尼所以不能無所折衷也。仲尼既歿，聖學榛蕪，戰國從衡，衆說蜂起。挾藝者吐舌而爭談，窮經者分門而肄辯，真偽溷淆，莫可究詰。於是秦人乘之，而坑焚之禍起矣。斯豈可獨
translation_en:
…such were they. Yixiang, the Scribe of the Left in Chu, could read the Three Tumuli (San fen), Five Canons (Wu dian), Eight Cords (Ba suo), and Nine Mounds (Jiu qiu): these, then, were the works that scholars and scholar-officials recited and studied. So rich was this cultural achievement that the same customs prevailed throughout the world, and all nine regions shared a common order. Those who produced works afterward could not equal it.

By the age of decline, however, elaborate literary ornament prevailed while substantial virtue waned; historical writings proliferated while divergent doctrines flourished. Zhongni feared that readers would lack a common understanding. He therefore clarified the ancient statutes, established rites and music, reduced the poems to three hundred, and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals from the historical records of Lu. He read the Way of the Changes to set aside the Eight Cords, and expounded the geographical account of the Director of the Bureau of Operations (Zhifang) to dispense with the Nine Mounds. He examined and discussed the ancient Tumuli and Canons, taking the eras of Tang and Yu as his starting point. Of the writings produced since the ancient sovereigns and the Si rulers of Xia [?], many were excised and left unrecorded. Could it be that these books contained nothing worth adopting? Rather, their times and customs were remote, the surviving traces lacked reliable foundations, and amid fragmentary texts and broken bamboo slips, spurious accounts confused the genuine.

Thus, those who advocated governing while tilling the fields alongside the people borrowed authority for their doctrines from Shennong; those who expounded yin and yang and medical prescriptions appropriated the words of Huangdi. Other discussions, such as those concerning the primordial simplicity and the primordial beginning, frequently wandered into falsehood and fantasy; books about the Three Sovereigns and the Ten Epochs were all far-fetched and fabulous. When events have no corroboration, those hearing of them are startled and alarmed; when statements have evidence, those studying them find understanding in their hearts. This is why Zhongni could not avoid weighing and adjudicating among them.

After Zhongni died, the learning of the sages became overgrown with weeds. During the Warring States period, advocates of vertical and horizontal alliances advanced competing doctrines in swarms. Those possessing specialized learning wagged their tongues in contentious discussion; those who investigated the classics divided into schools and practiced disputation. Truth and falsehood became mingled, beyond investigation or questioning. The men of Qin thereupon took advantage of this, and the calamity of burying scholars and burning books arose. How could this be attributed solely to …

…such was the case. Yixiang, the Recorder of the Left in Chu, could read the Three Tombs (Sanfen), Five Canons (Wudian), Eight Cords (Basuo), and Nine Mounds (Jiuqiu): these, then, were the works that scholars and high officials recited and studied. So splendid was this culture that the same customs prevailed throughout the world, and all nine regions shared a common order. No author of later times could equal it.

In the declining age, however, elaborate literary adornment prevailed while substantive virtue waned; historical writings multiplied while divergent doctrines flourished. Zhongni (Confucius), fearing that readers would lack a unified understanding, clarified the old statutes and established rites and music. He reduced the poems to three hundred and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals from the historical records of Lu. He read the teachings of the Changes to displace the Eight Cords, and set forth the Account of the Regions (Zhifang) to supersede the Nine Mounds.
